title: When to use LinkedList over ArrayList — decision guide
shortTitle: When should you use LinkedList over ArrayList?

s1_definition.profdef: Use **LinkedList** when: (1) You need a Deque — frequent addFirst/removeLast/addLast/removeFirst (but ArrayDeque is usually better). (2) You insert/remove elements during iteration using ListIterator (O(1) pointer update vs O(n) array shift). (3) You NEVER need random access by index. Use **ArrayList** for everything else — which is 95% of cases. ArrayList's cache locality (contiguous memory) makes it faster even for operations where LinkedList has better theoretical complexity.
s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayList: default choice (95%). LinkedList: only for ListIterator insert/remove during traversal. ArrayDeque beats LinkedList even as a Deque.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Use **LinkedList** when: (1) You need a Deque — frequent addFirst/removeLast/addLast/removeFirst (but ArrayDeque is usually better). (2) You insert/remove elements during iteration using ListIterator (O(1) pointer update vs O(n) array shift). (3) You NEVER need random access by index. Use **ArrayList** for everything else — which is 95% of cases. ArrayList's cache locality (contiguous memory) makes it faster even for operations where LinkedList has better theoretical complexity.

**One line to remember:** ArrayList: default choice (95%). LinkedList: only for ListIterator insert/remove during traversal. ArrayDeque beats LinkedList even as a Deque.

sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the engineering team hit a real problem that maps directly onto deciding when LinkedList beats ArrayList. Rajesh (account SAV2001, a software engineer with a savings balance of 1,000,000 rupees) and Priya (account CUR3001, a property owner with a current balance of 250,000 rupees) both run operations that stress the system's collection handling, and the wrong data-structure choice here caused slow lookups, lost entries, or incorrect ordering in production reports.

The mini-project below reproduces that banking scenario and shows exactly how deciding when LinkedList beats ArrayList solves it correctly, using BigDecimal for every money value and the same Account model with debit and credit behaviour.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a workload of frequent insertions and removals at the front of a list.

**Step 1.** Inserting a new transaction at the head of an `ArrayList` shifts every existing element one slot to the right, an O(n) operation.

**Step 2.** The same head insertion in a `LinkedList` only relinks a couple of node pointers, an O(1) operation.

**Step 3.** Because the workload is front-heavy with few random reads, the `LinkedList` is chosen, whereas index-based balance lookups would instead favour the ArrayList.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Use ArrayList as default. LinkedList only when: (1) frequent insert/remove at current iterator position, (2) you need both List and Deque interfaces on the same collection. ArrayDeque outperforms LinkedList for pure Deque/Stack use. LinkedList uses 5-10x more memory than ArrayList. Never use LinkedList for random access by index.

---

keyPoints: Frequent add/remove at head: LinkedList O(1) vs ArrayList O(n)
Queue/Deque behavior needed: LinkedList implements Deque
Large list with frequent inserts in middle at known iterator position
In practice: ArrayList wins 90%+ of the time due to cache locality
